messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Source: Piezoelectric (Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ || $C_p$ || $20\text{ M}\Omega$ leakage).
    *   Load: $R_L$ (from `out` to `0`).
    *   Goal: $V_{out}$ between $1.8\text{V}$ and $3.6\text{V}$, ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$, startup $\le 0.4\text{s}$, settled $\le 0.02\text{V}$ change.
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components.
    *   Operating Conditions: $S1$ (nominal), $S2$ (low f, mid load), $S3$ (high f, light load), $S4$ (low f, large $C_p$), $S5$ (high f, large $C_p$, heavy load), $S6$ (hot, heavy load).

    *   Reference FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) failed:
        *   $S2$: Ripple too high, Startup too slow.
        *   $S3$: $V_{max}$ too high ($4.2\text{V}$).
        *   $S4$: $V_{avg}$ too low ($1.79\text{V}$), Ripple too high, Startup too slow.
        *   $S5$: $V_{avg}$ too low ($1.74\text{V}$), Startup too slow.
        *   $S6$: $V_{avg}$ too low ($1.55\text{V}$), Startup too slow.
    *   The FBR is basically a passive rectifier. It's inefficient and the output voltage is directly tied to the piezo's open-circuit voltage minus diode drops. $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$.
        *   $S1: V_{oc} \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
        *   $S3: V_{oc} = 100\mu / (2\pi \cdot 200 \cdot 17.5\text{n}) \approx 4.5\text{V}$ (Explains $V_{max}$ failure).
        *   $S5: V_{oc} = 100\mu / (2\pi \cdot 200 \cdot 32.5\text{n}) \approx 2.4\text{V}$.
        *   $S6: V_{oc} = 50\mu / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{n}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$ (But heavy load $R_L=200\text{k}$ pulls it down).

    *   *Issue 1: Overvoltage ($S3$)* $\rightarrow$ Need a Zener clamp (DZ33) or a regulator.
    *   *Issue 2: Undervoltage/Startup ($S2, S4, S5, S6$)* $\rightarrow$ Need more efficiency or voltage boost.
    *   *Issue 3: Ripple ($S2, S4$)* $\rightarrow$ Need a larger storage capacitor or a better regulation scheme.

    *   **SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):** This is the gold standard for piezo harvesting. It flips the voltage across $C_p$ using an inductor at the peaks, effectively multiplying the voltage and increasing the power extracted.
    *   **SEP (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction):** Similar to SSHI, extracts charge at peaks.
    *   **Standard Rectifier with Zener Clamp:** Simplest fix for $S3$ but doesn't solve the power/startup issues for $S5, S6$.

    *   *Option 1: SSHI (Standard).*
        *   Piezo $\rightarrow$ Inductor $\rightarrow$ Switch (triggered at peaks) $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Storage C.
        *   Actually, a simpler version: Piezo $C_p$ is flipped via an inductor and switch at the voltage extremes, then rectified.
        *   Circuit: Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`. Inductor $L1$ between `pzp` and a switch $S1$. $S1$ between `pzp` and `pzn` (to flip) or `pzp` and `out`. Wait, the standard SSHI flip is across the piezo.
        *   Wait, a common simplified SSHI is: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Full-Bridge $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$. To add the flip: an inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo. When $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate.

    *   *Option 2: Half-Wave/Full-Wave Rectifier with Zener Clamp.*
        *   FBR + DZ33 on `out`. This fixes $S3$ but doesn't help $S5, S6$.

    *   *Option 3: Parallel SSHI / SECE.*
        *   Let's try a basic SSHI flip:
            *   Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`.
            *   Inductor $L1$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
            *   Switch $S1$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
            *   Control $G1$: `edges` = "both", `ton` $\approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.
            *   This flips the voltage across the piezo.
            *   Then we need to rectify the flipped voltage.
            *   Full bridge: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`, `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`, `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`, `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (incorrect).
            *   Correct FBR nodes: `D1: [pzp, out]`, `D2: [pzn, out]`, `D3: [0, pzp]`, `D4: [0, pzn]`. (Wait, these are the diodes).

    *   *Refining the SSHI:*
        1.  $L1$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
        2.  $S1$ from `n1` to `pzn` (controlled by $G1$ "both" edges).
        3.  Rectifier:
            *   $D1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
            *   $D2$: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
            *   $D3$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (Wait, the FBR is 4 diodes. $D3, D4$ usually return to 0).
            *   $D3$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` is wrong. It should be `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `0`? No, the return path is `0`.
            *   FBR layout: $D1: [pzp, out]$, $D2: [pzn, out]$, $D3: [0, pzp]$ is wrong. It's $D3: [pzp, 0]$? No, the reference design said: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`. This is confusing. Let's re-read. "return diodes have their anode on ground".
            *   So: $D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]$.
            *   Wait, $D3: [0, pzp]$ means anode at $0$, cathode at `pzp`. This allows current to flow from $0$ to `pzp` when `pzp` is negative. Correct.

    *   *Adding Zener for $S3$:*
        *   $DZ33$: `[0, out]`.

    *   *Calculations for SSHI:*
        *   $C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
        *   $L = 10\text{mH}$.
        *   $T_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx \pi \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
        *   This fits in the $1\mu\text{s}$ limit? No, $T_{on}$ limit is $0.001\text{s}$ ($1\text{ms}$). So $50\mu\text{s}$ is fine.

    *   **Design A: SSHI + FBR + Zener**
        *   $L1: [pzp, n1]$, $S1: [n1, pzn]$, $G1: \{edges: both, ton: 50\mu s\}$.
        *   $D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]$ (DSCH).
        *   $D_{z}: [0, out]$ (DZ33).
        *   $C_{out}: [out, 0]$.
        *   Rationale: SSHI increases power extraction (fixes $S5, S6, S2, S4$), Zener clamps voltage (fixes $S3$).

    *   **Design B: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   SECE is usually an inductor and a switch that connects the piezo to the storage cap at the peaks.
        *   $L1: [pzp, n1]$, $S1: [n1, out]$.
        *   Wait, SECE is more complex. Let's try a simpler "Parallel-SSHI".
        *   Actually, let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" if we have enough switches.
        *   Alternatively, a simple Boost converter (though the SYNC is a fixed-timer, not a PWM controller, making a boost hard without a specific topology).

    *   **Design C: Basic FBR + Large Capacitor + Zener**
        *   Just in case the SSHI is too unstable. $C_{out}$ is optimized by the EA anyway.
        *   $D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn], D_z: [0, out], C_{out}: [out, 0]$.
        *   Rationale: See if the Zener alone fixes the $S3$ failure and if a larger $C_{out}$ fixes the ripple.

    *   *S1: nominal* - Should be fine.
    *   *S2: low freq, mid load* - $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$. FBR might struggle with startup/ripple. SSHI helps power.
    *   *S3: high freq, light load* - $V_{oc} \approx 4.5\text{V}$. Zener is essential here.
    *   *S4: low freq, large $C_p$* - $V_{oc} \approx 3.1\text{V}$. Power is low. SSHI helps.
    *   *S5: high freq, large $C_p$, heavy load* - $V_{oc} \approx 2.4\text{V}$. Diode drops (0.5V) might leave only 1.9V. Very tight. SSHI is necessary to boost the internal voltage.
    *   *S6: hot, heavy load* - $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$. Heavy load. SSHI helps.

    *   The most promising is SSHI.
    *   Component list for Design A:
        *   $L1$: `[pzp, n1]`
        *   $S1$: `[n1, pzn]` (ctrl: $G1$)
        *   $G1$: `SYNC` (edges: both, ton: $50\mu\text{s}$, phase: 0)
        *   $D1$: `[pzp, out]` (DSCH)
        *   $D2$: `[pzn, out]` (DSCH)
        *   $D3$: `[0, pzp]` (DSCH)
        *   $D4$: `[0, pzn]` (DSCH)
        *   $D_{z}$: `[0, out]` (DZ33)
        *   $C1$: `[out, 0]`
        *   Total: 9 components.

    *   Wait, is the $S1$ switch correctly placed?
        In a standard SSHI (Parallel), the inductor and switch are in parallel with the piezo to flip the charge.
        When the piezo voltage reaches $V_{peak}$, the switch closes, and $L$ and $C_p$ exchange energy: $V_{Cp} \rightarrow -V_{Cp}$.
        Then the rectifier sends the current to $C_{out}$.
        The FBR handles the rectification.

    *   *Alternative SSHI topology (Series):*
        Inductor in series with the rectifier.
        $L1: [pzp, n1]$, $S1: [n1, out]$.
        This is more like SECE.

    *   Let's stick to the Parallel-SSHI flip + FBR.

    *   Wait, if I use a Zener, I must be careful not to kill all the power. DZ33 conducts at 3.3V. The load min is 1.8V and max 3.6V. 3.3V is a safe clamping point.

    *   $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ (nominal). $L = 10\text{mH}$.
    *   $T_{on} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p} = 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-7}} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
    *   The $C_p$ varies from $17.5\text{nF}$ to $32.5\text{nF}$.
    *   $T_{on}$ for $17.5\text{nF} \approx 41\mu\text{s}$.
    *   $T_{on}$ for $32.5\text{nF} \approx 56\mu\text{s}$.
    *   $50\mu\text{s}$ is a good starting point for the EA to optimize.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener (High Power)*
    *   *Design 2: FBR + Zener (Simple/Stable)*
    *   *Design 3: SSHI (without Zener, just to see)* - Actually, $S3$ will fail. Let's try an SSHI with a different rectification (half-bridge) to save components or change the flip logic. Let's go with a modified SSHI where the switch is only on one edge to see if it's more stable. No, "both" is generally better.

    Let's reconsider Design 3. Maybe a "Charge Pump" style or "SECE"?
    SECE: $L1$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S1$ from `n1` to `out`.
    This extracts charge $Q = C_p \cdot V_{peak}$ into the output capacitor.
    $G1$ should trigger at "both" edges.

    *   Design 1 (SSHI-Parallel): `L1:[pzp,n1], S1:[n1,pzn], G1:both, FBR, Dz, C1`.
    *   Design 2 (FBR-Zener): `FBR, Dz, C1`.
    *   Design 3 (SECE-ish): `L1:[pzp,n1], S1:[n1,out], G1:both, D1:[out,n1], FBR, Dz, C1`. (Wait, too complex).

    Let's keep it simple.
    1. Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    2. FBR + Zener.
    3. Parallel SSHI + Half-bridge (to see if efficiency is higher).

    Wait, a half-bridge rectifier is just 2 diodes. $D1: [pzp, out], D3: [0, pzp]$? No.
    Half-bridge: $D1: [pzp, out], C1: [out, 0]$. This only takes the positive half.
    Given the piezo is a current source, we really want both halves.

    Let's refine the Parallel SSHI components for Proposal 1:
    L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn], G1: SYNC, D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn], Dz: [0, out], C1: [out, 0].

    Let's refine Proposal 2 (FBR + Zener):
    D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn], Dz: [0, out], C1: [out, 0].

    Let's refine Proposal 3 (SSHI-Single Edge):
    L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn], G1: SYNC(edges: pos), D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn], Dz: [0, out], C1: [out, 0].

    Wait, one more thing. The "FBR" in the reference design used 4 DSCH diodes. Let's make sure I use DSCH for those and DZ33 for the clamp.

    Let's double-check the FBR connections again:
    `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`
    This is:
    D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
    D2: pzn $\rightarrow$ out
    D3: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp
    D4: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn
    Current paths:
    If pzp is positive: $0 \rightarrow \text{Piezo} \rightarrow pzp \rightarrow D1 \rightarrow out \rightarrow R_L \rightarrow 0$. (Correct)
    If pzp is negative (pzn is positive): $0 \rightarrow \text{Piezo} \rightarrow pzn \rightarrow D2 \rightarrow out \rightarrow R_L \rightarrow 0$. (Correct)
    Wait, the return path is the piezo itself. Let's trace:
    When $pzp$ is high, $pzn$ is low.
    Current flows from $pzp$ through $D1$ to $out$.
    Where does it return? It must return to the piezo's $pzn$ terminal.
    So current flows from $out$ through $R_L$ to $0$, then from $0$ through $D4$ to $pzn$.
    So the loop is: $pzp \rightarrow D1 \rightarrow out \rightarrow R_L \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow D4 \rightarrow pzn \rightarrow \text{Piezo} \rightarrow pzp$.
    This is a complete loop. The 4-diode bridge is correct.
